attribute_or_claim: Base Temperature & GDD Calculation
recorded_value_or_summary: The standard thermal base temperature (Tbase) for wheat phenology modeling is 0.0°C (32.0°F). GDD is calculated as ((Tmax + Tmin)/2) - Tbase. McMaster and Wilhelm demonstrate that Method 1 (resetting daily mean to Tbase if < Tbase) and Method 2 (resetting individual Tmax/Tmin to Tbase if < Tbase) can diverge by up to 83% in cold seasons.
source_title: Growing degree-days: one equation, two interpretations
limitations: Agro-meteorological modeling standard; models must explicitly specify whether Method 1 or Method 2 is applied.

attribute_or_claim: Spring Wheat Thermal Time Accumulation

source_title: Use of Growing-Degree Days to Determine Spring Wheat Growth Stages
author_or_institution: Bauer, A., Fanning, C., Enz, J.W., Eberlein, C.V.

geographic_scope: Northern Great Plains (ND, MN, SD, MT)

attribute_or_claim: Winter Wheat Growth Staging & Phenology

Total spring thermal time: ~1,300-1,750 GDD-C (base 0°C).
source_organization: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension Service
source_title: Wheat Growth and Development
citation_location: Publication MF3300, Visual Chart and Technical Narrative
geographic_scope: U.S. Central and Southern Great Plains

attribute_or_claim: Seasonal Water Use & Peak ETc (Winter Wheat)
recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal crop water use (ETc) for winter wheat in the Central Plains ranges from 15 to 25 inches (380 to 635 mm), with typical benchmark trials averaging 17.7 to 23.4 inches (450 to 600 mm). Peak daily water use occurs during heading through grain fill, averaging 0.30 to 0.35 inches/day (7.6 to 8.9 mm/day), with single-day evaporative demand reaching 0.40 to 0.54 inches/day under hot, windy conditions.
source_organization: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension Service
source_title: Agricultural Crop Water Use
geographic_scope: U.S. Central and Southern Great Plains (Kansas, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Texas High Plains)
limitations: In dryland systems without irrigation, actual ET is bounded by precipitation and available stored subsoil water.

attribute_or_claim: Seasonal Water Use & Root Zone (Spring Wheat)
recorded_value_or_summary: Hard red spring wheat requires 12 to 16 inches (305 to 406 mm) of seasonal water (ETc) to reach full yield potential, extending to 16-18 inches (400-450 mm) under high-yield irrigation. Active root zone depth spans 42 to 48 inches (107 to 122 cm), with effective managed extraction focused in the top 36 inches (91 cm). Water use averages ~1.5 inches per Haun stage between 8-leaf and kernel hard maturity.
source_organization: North Dakota Agricultural Experiment Station / USDA-ARS Northern Great Plains Research Laboratory
source_title: Soil water use by plant development stage of spring and winter wheat
author_or_institution: Bauer, A., Black, A.L., Frank, A.B.
citation_location: Experiment Station Bulletin No. 519, Tables 4-7, pp. 8-16
geographic_scope: Northern Great Plains (North Dakota, South Dakota, Eastern Montana, Western Minnesota)

attribute_or_claim: Nutrient Removal Rates & Seed Safety
recorded_value_or_summary: Per bushel of harvested wheat grain (60 lb): removal is 0.50 lb P2O5/bu and 0.25 lb K2O/bu. attribute_or_claim: Spring Wheat Nitrogen Fertility & Protein Target
recorded_value_or_summary: Spring wheat nitrogen recommendations in the Northern Plains use an economic optimal N approach targeting maximum net return rather than maximum yield. Grain protein benchmark is 14.0% to prevent market dockage. N recommendations require a 0- to 24-inch profile soil nitrate-N test, subtracting residual nitrate-N and previous crop credits from total regional N needs. Base N need ranges from 2.2 to 2.5 lb total available N per bushel in western ND to 2.0-2.2 lb N/bu in eastern ND.
source_title: Fertilizing Hard Red Spring Wheat and Durum
geographic_scope: Northern Great Plains (North Dakota, South Dakota, Minnesota, Montana)
limitations: Excessive N increases risk of lodging and lodging-induced foliar diseases without increasing yield.

attribute_or_claim: Winter Wheat Fertility & Soil Test Interpretation
recorded_value_or_summary: Kansas winter wheat total nitrogen requirement is calculated as 2.4 lb N per bushel of realistic yield goal. Net fertilizer N is calculated by subtracting 0- to 24-inch profile nitrate-N, organic matter mineralization credit (10-20 lb N per % OM depending on region), and previous crop credits. Soil test phosphorus critical level is 20 ppm (Bray P-1 or Mehlich-3); potassium critical level is 130 ppm exchangeable K.

attribute_or_claim: Residue Biomass & C:N Ratio
recorded_value_or_summary: Wheat straw has a typical carbon-to-nitrogen (C:N) ratio of approximately 80:1 (range 60:1 to 100:1). Semi-dwarf wheat has a harvest index (HI) of 0.40 to 0.48, generating ~1.0 to 1.3 lb of straw residue per pound of grain (~60-80 lb residue per bushel). A 60 bu/acre grain yield produces 3,600-4,800 lb/acre dry residue. Because the C:N ratio far exceeds the microbial threshold of ~24:1, decomposition causes temporary soil inorganic N immobilization.
source_organization: USDA-NRCS East National Technology Support Center
source_title: Carbon to Nitrogen Ratios in Cropping Systems
citation_location: Soil Quality Technical Note No. 1, Table 1 & Narrative, pp. 1-3
limitations: Actual straw C:N varies with nitrogen fertility and drought stress at maturity.

attribute_or_claim: Spring Freeze Injury Thresholds (Winter Wheat)
recorded_value_or_summary: Freeze sensitivity in winter wheat increases dramatically as plants de-harden in spring: Tillering (Feekes 4-5): 12°F (-11.1°C) for 2 hours causes leaf chlorosis/burn; Jointing (Feekes 6-8): 24°F (-4.4°C) for 2 hours causes growing point mortality and stem splitting; Boot (Feekes 10): 28°F (-2.2°C) for 2 hours causes head entrapment and floret sterility; Heading/Flowering (Feekes 10.5): 30°F (-1.1°C) for 2 hours kills male flower parts (anthers), causing complete floret sterility.
source_organization: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension Service
source_title: Spring Freeze Injury to Kansas Wheat
author_or_institution: Shroyer, J.P., Mikesell, M.E., Paulsen, G.M.
geographic_scope: U.S. Central and Southern Great Plains
limitations: Soil moisture, topography, and canopy density can buffer or exacerbate canopy air temperatures.

attribute_or_claim: Wheat Cardinal Temperatures
recorded_value_or_summary: Comprehensive review of cardinal temperatures for wheat: Vegetative development: Tbase = 0.0°C, Topt = 20.3°C, Tmax = 32.7°C. Anthesis (flowering): Tbase = 9.5°C, Topt = 21.0°C (range 19-22°C), Tmax = 31.0°C. Grain filling: Tbase = 9.2°C, Topt = 20.7°C (range 18-22°C), Tmax = 35.4°C. Temperatures >31°C during anthesis impair microsporogenesis and induce sterility; temperatures >35°C during grain filling deactivate starch synthase.
source_organization: European Journal of Agronomy / Agricultural and Forest Meteorology
source_title: Temperatures and the growth and development of wheat: a review
citation_location: Eur. J. Agron. 10(1):23-36 / Agric. For. Meteorol. 97(1):73-93, Table 2 & Table 4
limitations: Cardinal temperatures represent steady-state physiological responses; short episodic heat shocks have dynamic thresholds.

attribute_or_claim: Empirical Heat Stress Yield Threshold (Winter Wheat)
recorded_value_or_summary: Statistical analysis of 25 years of Kansas winter wheat variety performance trials identified a critical extreme heat threshold of 34°C during spring growth. Degree days accumulated above 34°C caused severe, non-linear yield reductions, whereas exposure between 15°C and 34°C was neutral or beneficial. Negative impacts of warming on winter wheat yields substantially outweighed benefits from reduced severe winter freezing.
source_organization: Kansas State University / University of Arkansas
source_title: Effect of warming temperatures on US wheat yields
author_or_institution: Tack, J., Barkley, A., Nalley, L.L.
geographic_scope: U.S. Central Great Plains (Kansas winter wheat production)
limitations: Empirical yield response threshold from historical Kansas data; should not be interpreted as a universal biological survival ceiling.

attribute_or_claim: Heat Stress at Anthesis & Grain Filling
recorded_value_or_summary: Daytime temperatures >= 31-35°C during anthesis (especially 5 days pre-anthesis through flowering) cause severe pollen sterility, impaired pollen tube elongation, and floret abortion, drastically reducing grain number per spike. High temperatures (>= 32-35°C) during grain filling accelerate leaf senescence, shorten the grain-filling period, and reduce thousand-kernel weight (TKW) by up to 5% per 1°C increase above 20°C.
source_organization: Kansas State University Department of Agronomy
source_title: Impact of high temperature stress on floret fertility and individual kernel weight of wheat
author_or_institution: Prasad, P.V.V., Pisipati, S.R., Ristic, Z., Bukovnik, U., Fritz, A.K.
limitations: Nighttime temperatures exacerbate daytime heat stress; elevated night temp (>= 20-24°C) increases dark respiration and carbon loss.

attribute_or_claim: Waterlogging Sensitivity & Hypoxia Timeline
recorded_value_or_summary: Wheat roots require soil oxygen for aerobic respiration; in waterlogged/saturated soil, oxygen depletion occurs within 24-48 hours. Exposure of 1 to 3 days is generally tolerated with temporary growth pauses if foliage is cool and unflooded; exposure of 3 to 7 days causes seminal root death, reduced tillering, and lower leaf chlorosis (due to impaired N uptake); waterlogging exceeding 7 to 14 days causes severe root necrosis,stand thinning, and 20% to 50% yield reduction depending on stage.
source_organization: Department of Agriculture Western Australia / University of Western Australia
source_title: Review of prospects for germplasm improvement for waterlogging tolerance in wheat, barley and oats
citation_location: Annals of Botany 91(2):145-162, Section: Plant Responses to Waterlogging, pp. 146-150
limitations: Waterlogging injury is heavily compounded by warm temperatures; cool winter waterlogging is tolerated longer than warm spring waterlogging.

attribute_or_claim: Salinity Tolerance (ECe Threshold & Slope)
recorded_value_or_summary: Wheat is classified as moderately tolerant to soil salinity. The baseline Maas-Hoffman electrical conductivity threshold (ECe) is 6.0 dS/m, with a yield reduction slope of 7.1% per dS/m increase above 6.0 dS/m (Yr = 100 - 7.1*(ECe - 6.0)). Semi-dwarf cultivars (Francois et al., 1986) demonstrate higher salt tolerance with a threshold of 8.6 dS/m and slope of 3.0% per dS/m. Wheat is significantly more salinity-tolerant than corn (threshold 1.7 dS/m) or soybean (threshold 5.0 dS/m).
source_organization: USDA Agricultural Research Service, U.S. Salinity Laboratory, Riverside, CA
source_title: Crop salt tolerance-current assessment
citation_location: ASCE J. Irrig. Drain. Div. 103(IR2):115-134, Table 1, p. 119
limitations: Seedling emergence stage is more sensitive to salinity than vegetative or ripening stages.

attribute_or_claim: Take-All Root Rot & Monoculture Penalties
recorded_value_or_summary: Take-all (Gaeumannomyces graminis var. tritici / G. tritici) is the primary root and crown disease in continuous wheat systems. A 1- to 2-year non-cereal broadleaf break crop (soybean, canola, field peas, sunflower) starves the soil-borne fungal inoculum, resulting in substantial yield benefits (15-30% yield boost over continuous wheat). Under continuous wheat monoculture, take-all peaks in years 2-4, followed by spontaneous biological suppression ('take-all decline' driven by 2,4-DAPG-producing fluorescent Pseudomonas spp.), though baseline yield remains below break-crop rotations.
source_organization: USDA Agricultural Research Service / American Phytopathological Society (APS Press)
source_title: Wheat Health Management
citation_location: APS Press Monograph, Chapter 4 (Roots and Soilborne Pathogens), pp. 53-72
geographic_scope: U.S. National Wheat Systems (especially PNW, Midwest, and Northern Plains)
limitations: Barley, triticale, and grassy weeds (e.g. bromes) serve as alternative hosts and maintain inoculum.

attribute_or_claim: Fusarium Head Blight Carryover from Corn
recorded_value_or_summary: Fusarium head blight (FHB / scab) in wheat is caused by Fusarium graminearum (Gibberella zeae), which also causes Gibberella stalk and ear rot in corn. Planting wheat directly into corn residue dramatically elevates FHB spore pressure during wheat flowering, leading to severe yield loss, tombstone kernels, and deoxynivalenol (DON / vomitoxin) contamination (>2.0 ppm triggers elevator dockage or rejection). Soybean is the preferred preceding crop for wheat, lowering localized inoculum and reducing FHB epidemic risk.
source_organization: Purdue University Extension / The Ohio State University Extension / Crop Protection Network
source_title: Fusarium Head Blight (Head Scab)
author_or_institution: Wise, K., Woloshun, C., Freije, A., Paul, P.
citation_location: Purdue Extension BP-33-W / CPN-1002, Disease Cycle & Management, pp. 1-4
geographic_scope: U.S. Midwest, Eastern Corn Belt, Northern Plains, and Mid-Atlantic
limitations: Soybean is a minor host for F. graminearum (causing damping-off/pod blight), but does not generate the massive ascospore loads that corn stalks produce.

attribute_or_claim: Wheat Streak Mosaic Virus & Volunteer Green Bridge
recorded_value_or_summary: Wheat streak mosaic virus (WSMV) is transmitted exclusively by the wheat curl mite (Aceria tosichella). The mite and virus require a continuous 'green bridge' of living host tissue to survive between summer wheat harvest and fall wheat emergence. Volunteer wheat is the primary summer reservoir. To break the disease cycle, all volunteer wheat and grassy weeds must be completely terminated via herbicides or tillage at least 2 weeks (ideally 30+ days) prior to planting fall winter wheat so mites starve and desiccate.
source_organization: Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station and Cooperative Extension Service
source_title: Wheat Streak Mosaic
author_or_institution: De Wolf, E., Andersen Onofre, K., Michaud, J.P.
citation_location: Publication EP167, Disease Cycle & Control Measures, pp. 1-4
geographic_scope: U.S. Great Plains (Kansas, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Colorado, Montana, South Dakota, Texas)
limitations: Corn and some summer annual grasses (e.g. foxtails) can host curl mites, though volunteer wheat is by far the primary epidemiological vector.

attribute_or_claim: Dual-Purpose Grazing & First Hollow Stem Stage
recorded_value_or_summary: In the Southern Great Plains (OK, TX, KS), dual-purpose winter wheat is planted early (late Aug - early Sept) for cattle grazing from November through early spring, followed by grain harvest. The physiological cutoff for cattle removal is First Hollow Stem (FHS), defined as 1.5 cm (5/8 inch, diameter of a dime) of hollow stem developing below the embryonic head. Grazing past FHS damages the developing spike and reduces subsequent grain yield by 1% to 5% per day.
source_title: First Hollow Stem: A Critical Wheat Growth Stage for Dual-Purpose Producers
author_or_institution: de Oliveira Silva, A., Edwards, J.T.
geographic_scope: U.S. Southern Great Plains (Oklahoma, Texas Panhandle, Southern Kansas)
limitations: Earlier planting for forage increases susceptibility to fall armyworm, Hessian fly, and wheat streak mosaic virus.

attribute_or_claim: Double-Cropping Winter Wheat & Soybean
recorded_value_or_summary: Double-cropping winter wheat followed immediately by soybean is widely viable south of approximately 39°N to 40°N latitude (Kentucky, southern Illinois/Indiana, Missouri, Arkansas, Tennessee, Virginia, Kansas). Primary limiting factors are late-season moisture depletion by maturing wheat and shortened soybean photoperiod. Delaying double-crop soybean planting past late June / early July imposes a yield penalty of 0.5 to 1.0 bushel/acre per day of delay. Harvesting wheat at 18-20% grain moisture and artificial drying accelerates soybean seeding by 3-5 days.
source_organization: University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension Service
source_title: Double-Cropping Wheat and Soybeans
author_or_institution: Lee, C., Herbek, J., Mansfield, K.
citation_location: University of Kentucky Bulletin ID-185, Chapters 1-3, pp. 5-14
geographic_scope: U.S. Mid-South, Ohio Valley, Southern Corn Belt (latitudes < 39-40°N)
limitations: In drought years, double-crop soybean stands fail to emerge or suffer severe summer abortion.

attribute_or_claim: Soil Acidity & Aluminum Toxicity Threshold
recorded_value_or_summary: Wheat grows optimally between soil pH 6.0 and 7.5. When soil pH drops below 5.5, insoluble aluminum-containing minerals dissolve into toxic trivalent aluminum (Al3+). Free Al3+ inhibits cell division in wheat root tips, causing short, stubby, brown, club-shaped roots, severe stunting, and impaired P uptake. Liming is triggered when soil pH falls below 5.5 to neutralize Al3+ and restore root elongation. Certain varieties carry ALMT1 (aluminum-activated malate transporter) genes conferring moderate low-pH tolerance.
source_title: Managing Acid Soils for Wheat Production
author_or_institution: Zhang, H., Raun, W., Edwards, J.T.
geographic_scope: U.S. Southern Great Plains, Eastern Washington Palouse, and Southeast
limitations: Surface-applied lime without tillage in no-till fields takes several years to neutralize subsoil acidity.

attribute_or_claim: Herbicide Rotational Restrictions & pH Dependency
recorded_value_or_summary: Rotational plant-back intervals for wheat and rotational crops following wheat are strictly product-label specific: Fomesafen (Flexstar, EPA Reg. No. 100-1101) mandates a 4.5-month plant-back interval for small grains (wheat). Atrazine (AAtrex 4L, EPA Reg. No. 100-497) restricts fall-seeded small grains following corn/sorghum application. In wheat, sulfonylurea herbicides like chlorsulfuron (Finesse/Glean) degrade via chemical hydrolysis, which is severely retarded in high pH soils (pH > 7.0 to 7.9). In alkaline soils, chlorsulfuron persistence can exceed 24 to 36 months, prohibiting rotation to sensitive broadleaves (sunflower, sorghum, non-STS soybean).
source_organization: U.S. EPA / K-State Research and Extension
source_title: EPA Pesticide Product Labels & Extension Weed Management Guides
author_or_institution: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency / Syngenta / Corteva / K-State Extension
citation_location: EPA Reg. Nos. 100-1101, 100-497, 352-522, 279-3610; KSU Chem. Weed Control MF258
limitations: Product formulations, tank mixes, and regional supplemental labels establish exact legal intervals.

attribute_or_claim: Spring Wheat Staging & Management Windows
recorded_value_or_summary: Spring wheat development progresses continuously across 85-115 days without winter dormancy: Germination/Emergence (Zadoks 00-10, 7-14 days), Tillering (Zadoks 20-29, 2-4 weeks), Stem Elongation / Jointing (Zadoks 30-39, 2-3 weeks; critical for final weed control and jointing-stage growth regulator application), Booting and Heading (Zadoks 40-59, 1-2 weeks), Anthesis (Zadoks 60-69, 3-5 days; critical window for triazole fungicide application to manage Fusarium head blight), and Milk/Dough Ripening (Zadoks 70-92, 4-5 weeks to physiological maturity indicated by complete loss of green color from peduncle).
source_title: Growth and Development Guide for Spring Wheat
author_or_institution: Simmons, S.R., Oelke, E.A., Anderson, P.M.
citation_location: Extension Folder AG-FO-2547, Zadoks & Feekes Scale Descriptions, pp. 1-12
geographic_scope: U.S. Northern Plains and Upper Midwest

attribute_or_claim: Residue Cover, Water Conservation, & Soil Carbon
recorded_value_or_summary: Standing wheat stubble traps winter snow, reduces wind speed at the soil surface by 50-70%, and suppresses soil evaporation during subsequent fallow or early growth of following crops. In Great Plains ecofallow/no-till systems, maintaining wheat residue increases soil water storage efficiency by 15-25% over conventional tillage. While surface residue decomposes slowly due to high C:N, long-term soil organic carbon (SOC) accrual is heavily driven by below-ground fine root turnover rather than straw alone, with humification efficiency of straw carbon typically limited to 8-15%.
source_title: Tillage, nitrogen, and cropping system effects on soil carbon sequestration
author_or_institution: Halvorson, A.D., Wienhold, B.J., Black, A.L.
citation_location: Soil Science Society of America Journal / Agronomy Journal 94(3):442-449, pp. 445-448
geographic_scope: U.S. Great Plains and Pacific Northwest Dryland Systems
limitations: SOC sequestration rates vary with baseline soil texture, initial carbon content, and precipitation.
