attribute_or_claim: Cotton-Sorghum Rotational Compatibility in High Plains
recorded_value_or_summary: Rotating cotton with grain sorghum breaks cotton root-knot nematode and Verticillium wilt; sorghum residue protects light sandy soils from wind erosion.
source_title: Long-term Cotton and Grain Sorghum Cropping Systems in the Rolling Plains of Texas
author_or_institution: DeLaune, P.B., Sij, J.W., Park, S.C., and Krutz, L.J.
geographic_scope: Texas Rolling Plains & Southern High Plains
limitations: Manage sorghum residue N tie-up in early spring.

attribute_or_claim: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates for Cotton
recorded_value_or_summary: Texas: Plant April 15 – June 20, Harvest Sept 15 – Dec 15; Mississippi/Delta: Plant April 25 – May 25, Harvest Sept 20 – Nov 10; Georgia/Southeast: Plant April 20 – May 31, Harvest Oct 1 – Dec 1.
source_title: Field Crops: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates, Agricultural Handbook No. 628
limitations: Cold wet soils at planting induce severe seedling disease (Pythium, Rhizoctonia) and stand failure.

attribute_or_claim: Deficit Drip Irrigation & Water Productivity in Texas High Plains
recorded_value_or_summary: Subsurface drip irrigation (SDI) delivers 250–500 mm net irrigation, boosting water use efficiency to 0.4–0.8 kg lint/m³ and minimizing evaporative losses.
source_title: Cotton Yield and Water Use Efficiency under Subsurface Drip Irrigation (Bordovsky & Mustian 2004)
limitations: High capital setup cost; rodent damage to drip tape during winter.

attribute_or_claim: Taxonomy, Subspecies, Growth Habit & USDA Symbol
recorded_value_or_summary: Oryza sativa L. (Symbol: ORSA), Poaceae, semi-aquatic C3 annual grass; Southern long-grain (indica) and California medium-grain (japonica).
source_title: The PLANTS Database
limitations: Strictly lowland/flooded rice; excludes upland wild rice (Zizania palustris L.).

attribute_or_claim: Phenology, DD50 Thermal Units & Water Seeding / Drill Seeding Systems
recorded_value_or_summary: 105–140 active growth days; DD50 base temp 10.0°C (50°F); 2,100–2,800 DD50-F (1,167–1,556 GDD-C) to harvest maturity; drill-seeded delayed flood and water-seeded systems.
source_organization: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
source_title: Arkansas Rice Production Handbook, Extension Bulletin MP192
citation_location: UADA MP192 'Rice Growth and Development' pp. 11–24
limitations: Late-planted rice exposed to fall cool snaps during flowering causes high blanking.

attribute_or_claim: Thermal Thresholds, Cold Blanking & Heat-Induced Chalkiness
recorded_value_or_summary: T_base 10.0°C, optimum 25–33°C, cold blanking threshold <15.0°C at microsporogenesis, heat stress >35°C (night >24°C impairs milling quality and head rice yield).
source_organization: University of California Davis / International Rice Research Institute
source_title: Rice Production Manual (UC Davis Pub 21623) & Board, J.E. (Cold Blanking in California Rice)
author_or_institution: Linquist, B.A., Mutters, R.G., and Greer, C.A.
citation_location: UC Davis Pub 21623 pp. 15–28; Agron. J. 72:483–487
limitations: Mid-South long grains highly sensitive to nighttime heat stress during grain filling (>24°C).

attribute_or_claim: Consumptive Water Use (ETc), Flood Irrigation Dynamics & Anoxia Adaptation
recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 700–900 mm (28–35 in); total water input 750–1,500 mm (30–60 in); 100% irrigated; highly flood-tolerant via aerenchyma; extremely sensitive to drought.
source_title: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 33 & Henry et al. (2016) Water Management in Rice
author_or_institution: Doorenbos, J. and Kassam, A.H. (FAO) / Henry, C.G.
citation_location: FAO 33 Section 'Rice' pp. 125–130; UADA MP192 pp. 75–94
limitations: Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) saves water but requires strict monitoring to prevent yield decline.

attribute_or_claim: Soil pH, Anaerobic Soil Chemistry, Impermeable Hardpan & Salinity Threshold
recorded_value_or_summary: Optimal pH 5.5–6.8 (neutralizes toward 6.5–7.0 under submergence); tolerated 4.8–7.8; Salinity threshold ECe 3.0 dS/m (moderately sensitive), slope 12.0% per dS/m; requires impermeable hardpan.
source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977) & Slaton et al. (Rice Soil Fertility)
author_or_institution: Maas, E.V. and Hoffman, G.J. / Slaton, N.A. et al.
citation_location: J. Irrig. Drain. Div. 103:115–134; UADA MP192 pp. 45–62
limitations: Alkaline or calcareous soils (pH >7.5) cause severe zinc deficiency (seedling chlorosis) upon flooding.

attribute_or_claim: Root Architecture, Effective Extraction Depth & Aerenchyma Tissue
recorded_value_or_summary: Effective water extraction depth 30–60 cm (1.0–2.0 ft); maximum anatomical penetration 60–90 cm (2.0–3.0 ft); superficial adventitious root mat with continuous aerenchyma.
source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & Yoshida (1981) Fundamentals of Rice Crop Science
limitations: Restricted root volume makes plants extremely vulnerable if flood is lost.

attribute_or_claim: Nutrient Removal, Anaerobic Nitrogen Dynamics & Urea Management
recorded_value_or_summary: Removal per 45 lb bushel: 0.60 lb N (13.3 kg N/t), 0.30 lb P2O5 (6.7 kg P2O5/t), 0.18 lb K2O (4.0 kg K2O/t); requires ammonium-forming N (urea); nitrate denitrifies rapidly.
source_organization: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
source_title: Rice Soil Fertility and Fertilizer Recommendations, MP192 Chapter 7
author_or_institution: Slaton, N.A., Roberts, T.L., and Hardke, J.T.
limitations: Nitrate forms of nitrogen cannot be used under flooded conditions due to total denitrification.

attribute_or_claim: Biomass Production, High Silica Residue, C:N Ratio & Net N Balance
recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass 7,000–11,000 kg/ha; C:N ratio 50:1–70:1; residue N 0.6–0.9%; residue N content 45–75 kg N/ha; net soil N balance -130 to -80 kg N/ha; credit 0 lb N/ac; high silica (10–15%).
source_title: Rice Straw Management and Decomposition in Temperate Lowlands (Linquist et al. 2006)
author_or_institution: Linquist, B.A. et al. / Bird, J.A. and Horwath, W.R.
limitations: Excessive straw under cold water generates organic acids and hydrogen sulfide toxic to seedling roots.

attribute_or_claim: Continuous Rice Monoculture Penalty, Sheath Blight & Red Rice
recorded_value_or_summary: Continuous rice causes 10–25% yield loss; drives rapid buildup of sheath blight (Rhizoctonia solani), weedy red rice (Oryza sativa f. spontanea), and straighthead disorder.
source_title: Rice Disease Management (MP192 Chapter 11) & Louisiana Rice Production Handbook
author_or_institution: Hardke, J.T., Cartwright, R.D., and Groth, D.E.
citation_location: UADA MP192 pp. 115–136; LSU AgCenter Pub. 2321
limitations: Requires rotating to soybean or using Clearfield/FullPage/Provisia herbicide-tolerant systems.

attribute_or_claim: Rice-Soybean Rotational Synergy in the Mid-South
recorded_value_or_summary: Rice-Soybean rotation (1:1 or 2:1) is the premier Mid-South system; allows selective grass/red rice control with ALS/ACCase herbicides and improves soil drainage.
source_organization: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
source_title: Economic and Agronomic Benefits of Rice-Soybean Crop Rotations, Research Series 581
limitations: Soybean yields on heavy clay rice soils depend critically on timely furrow irrigation.

attribute_or_claim: Herbicide Sensitivities & Carryover Restrictions in Rice
recorded_value_or_summary: Rice is sensitive to atrazine (18-month plant-back under flood), fomesafen, and ALS carryover; Clearfield (imidazolinone) rice carries strict plant-back rules.
source_organization: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
source_title: Recommended Weed Control for Arkansas Field Crops, MP44
author_or_institution: Norsworthy, J.K., Barber, L.T., and Hardke, J.T.
limitations: Stewardship agreements mandate rotating Clearfield rice to non-Clearfield crops to prevent outcrossing with red rice.

attribute_or_claim: Rice-Wheat Rotational Sequencing in the Delta
recorded_value_or_summary: Winter wheat can be seeded after early rice harvest, but late harvest or rutted waterlogged clay soils impede wheat stand establishment.
source_title: Rice-Wheat Cropping Systems in the Gulf Coast, Pub. 2844
limitations: Poorly drained heavy clay soils frequently waterlog wheat seedlings, causing severe stand loss.

attribute_or_claim: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates for Rice
recorded_value_or_summary: Arkansas: Plant April 10 – May 25, Harvest Aug 25 – Oct 15; California: Plant April 25 – May 20, Harvest Sept 15 – Nov 1; Louisiana: Plant March 15 – April 30, Harvest July 20 – Sept 15.
source_title: Field Crops: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates, Agricultural Handbook No. 628
limitations: Spring flood delays or high river stages delay field entry.

attribute_or_claim: Row Rice / Furrow-Irrigated Rice (FIR) System Adaptation
recorded_value_or_summary: Furrow-irrigated rice eliminates continuous levees, reducing water use by 15–30% and facilitating rotation with corn and soybean.
source_organization: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture
source_title: Furrow-Irrigated Rice Handbook, Extension Bulletin MP562
author_or_institution: Henry, C.G., Hardke, J.T., and Chlapecka, Z.
geographic_scope: Arkansas, Mississippi, and Missouri Bootheel Delta
limitations: Requires blast-resistant hybrids and split nitrogen management to maintain yield parity with flooded rice.

attribute_or_claim: Taxonomy, Row Types, Growth Habit & USDA Symbol
recorded_value_or_summary: Hordeum vulgare L. (Symbol: HOVU), Poaceae, cool-season C3 cereal; 2-row and 6-row types; Spring and Winter growth habits.
source_title: The PLANTS Database
limitations: Strictly domesticated barley; excludes wild barley (Hordeum spontaneum).

attribute_or_claim: Phenology, GDD Base Temperature & Vernalization Habits
recorded_value_or_summary: Active growth: Spring 70–95 d, Winter 115–150 d; Calendar: Spring 85–110 d, Winter 210–270 d; GDD base 0.0°C; Vernalization: Spring 0 d, Winter 30–50 d at 0–7°C (Vrn-H1 regulation).
source_organization: Montana State University Extension / North Dakota State University
source_title: Barley Growth and Development, EB0161 & NDSU Extension A-540
author_or_institution: Wiersma, J.J. et al. / Franck, S.
citation_location: MSU EB0161 pp. 1–8; NDSU A-540 pp. 1–12
geographic_scope: Northern Great Plains, Intermountain West, and Mid-Atlantic
limitations: Winter barley is less cold-hardy than winter wheat (-12 to -15°C vs -20°C kill threshold).

attribute_or_claim: Malting Quality Standards & Protein Thresholds
recorded_value_or_summary: AMBA malting specifications: grain protein 11.5–13.5% (>13.5% rejected to feed); plump kernels >80%; germination energy >95%; DON <1.0 ppm.
source_title: Malting Barley Quality Factors and Evaluation Standards
limitations: Strict rejection thresholds make nitrogen and irrigation management precision-critical.

attribute_or_claim: Thermal Thresholds, Anthesis Heat Sensitivity & Frost Limits
recorded_value_or_summary: T_base 0.0°C, optimum 15–22°C, heat stress >28–30°C (shrivels kernels, spikes protein), empirical breakpoint 29–30°C; frost limit: spring -4 to -6°C, winter -12 to -15°C.
source_title: Heat stress impacts on grain development in barley & Schlenker & Roberts (2009)
author_or_institution: Wallwork, M.A.B. et al. / Schlenker, W. and Roberts, M.J.
limitations: Spring barley avoids heat by early heading, but late-planted crops suffer heavy malting rejection.

attribute_or_claim: Consumptive Water Use (ETc), Drought Escapement & Waterlogging Sensitivity
recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 350–550 mm (14–22 in); peak 5–7 mm/d at boot/heading; drought tolerant/escaping via short season; highly sensitive to waterlogging (most sensitive of small grains).
source_title: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper No. 33 & Barley Water Use, EB0161
author_or_institution: Doorenbos, J. and Kassam, A.H. (FAO) / Bauder, J.W.
limitations: Unsuitable for poorly drained clay soils or high-water-table positions.

attribute_or_claim: Soil pH, Acidity Sensitivity & Superior Salinity Tolerance
recorded_value_or_summary: Optimal pH 6.0–7.5; tolerated 5.5–8.5; Salinity threshold ECe 8.0 dS/m (the most salt-tolerant commercial grain crop), slope 5.0% per dS/m; highly sensitive to aluminum at pH <5.8.
source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977) & Fertilizer Guidelines for Montana Crops
author_or_institution: Maas, E.V. and Hoffman, G.J. / Jones, C. and Jacobsen, J.
citation_location: J. Irrig. Drain. Div. 103:115–134; MSU EB0161
limitations: Severe yield collapse occurs below pH 5.5 unless limed.

attribute_or_claim: Root Architecture, Effective Extraction Depth & Penetration
recorded_value_or_summary: Effective water extraction depth 75–120 cm (2.5–4.0 ft); maximum anatomical penetration 120–180 cm (4.0–6.0 ft); dense fibrous root system.
source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & Weaver (1926) Root Development of Field Crops
limitations: Subsoil acidity or compaction restricts roots to shallow layers.

attribute_or_claim: Grain Nutrient Removal Rates & Malting Nitrogen Management
recorded_value_or_summary: Removal per 48 lb bushel: 0.78 lb N (16.2 kg N/t), 0.38 lb P2O5 (7.9 kg P2O5/t), 0.25 lb K2O (5.2 kg K2O/t); Total uptake per bushel: 1.10–1.30 lb N.
source_organization: Montana State University Extension / North Dakota State University
source_title: Fertilizer Guidelines for Montana Crops, EB0161 & NDSU SF-723
author_or_institution: Jones, C. and Jacobsen, J. / Franzen, D.
citation_location: MSU EB0161 pp. 8–14; NDSU SF-723 pp. 1–6
limitations: Feed barley can utilize higher N rates (1.5 lb N/bu) for maximum yield.

attribute_or_claim: Biomass Production, Residue C:N, Decomposition & Net N Balance
recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass 4,000–7,000 kg/ha; C:N ratio 60:1–80:1; residue N 0.6–0.9%; residue N content 25–50 kg N/ha; net soil N balance -90 to -50 kg N/ha; credit 0 lb N/ac (immobilizes 15–30 lb N/ac).
source_organization: USDA-ARS Northern Great Plains Research Laboratory
source_title: Residue Management and Carbon Sequestration in Northern Great Plains Cropping Systems
author_or_institution: Halvorson, A.D., Wienhold, B.J., and Black, A.L.
limitations: Starter N required on subsequent crops planted into heavy barley stubble.

attribute_or_claim: Continuous Barley Monoculture Penalty, Scald & Net Blotch
recorded_value_or_summary: Continuous barley monoculture causes 15–30% yield loss; escalates stubble-borne net blotch (Pyrenophora teres), scald (Rhynchosporium secalis), and spot blotch (Cochliobolus sativus).
source_title: Barley Disease Management, Extension Bulletin PP-803
limitations: Requires multi-mode foliar fungicides and resistant varieties if rotated continuously.

attribute_or_claim: Corn-Barley Rotation & Fusarium Head Blight (Scab) Risk
recorded_value_or_summary: Planting barley following corn carries severe Fusarium Head Blight (Fusarium graminearum) risk; DON contamination >1.0 ppm causes total malting rejection.
source_organization: American Malting Barley Association / NDSU Extension
source_title: Managing Scab in Malting Barley, AMBA Technical Note
limitations: Strict caution: require scab-tolerant varieties and triazole fungicide at heading.

attribute_or_claim: Winter Barley-Double Crop Soybean Rotation Synergy
recorded_value_or_summary: Winter barley matures 1–2 weeks earlier than winter wheat, enabling double-crop soybean planting by early to mid-June with 100% full-season yield potential in Mid-Atlantic/Upper South.
source_organization: Virginia Cooperative Extension / Penn State Extension
source_title: Winter Barley as a Double-Crop Option, Pub. 424-035
author_or_institution: Thomason, W.E., Beahm, B.R., and Alley, M.M.
geographic_scope: Mid-Atlantic, Ohio Valley, and Upper South
limitations: Requires timely autumn barley seeding (late September to mid-October) to ensure winter survival.

attribute_or_claim: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates for Barley
recorded_value_or_summary: Spring Barley (ND, MT, ID): Plant April 15 – May 20, Harvest July 25 – Sept 10; Winter Barley (VA, PA, NC): Plant Sept 25 – Oct 30, Harvest June 5 – June 25.
source_title: Field Crops: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates, Agricultural Handbook No. 628
limitations: Spring planting delays severely impact malting quality.

attribute_or_claim: Barley-Wheat Sequential Cereal Rotational Risks
recorded_value_or_summary: Sequential small-grain rotations (Barley after Wheat or Wheat after Barley) share take-all root rot, Cephalosporium stripe, and risk volunteer contamination.
source_title: Cereal Rotations in the Pacific Northwest, PNW Bul. 560
limitations: Include broadleaf crops (canola, pulse, soybean) as intervening break crops.

attribute_or_claim: Botanical Taxonomy, Growth Duration & Portfolio Role of Cereal Rye
recorded_value_or_summary: Secale cereale L., Poaceae, diploid (2n=14), cool-season annual grass; 180-240 days cover crop, 240-280 days full grain.
source_title: The PLANTS Database: Secale cereale L.
limitations: Spring rye cultivars exist but comprise <2% of North American acreage.

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Fall Seeding, Vernalization & Spring Termination Windows
recorded_value_or_summary: GDD base 0.0-4.4°C; obligate vernalization (30-60 d at 0-7°C); cumulative GDD to boot 900-1200, to grain 1800-2200.
source_organization: Purdue University Extension / Midwest Cover Crops Council
source_title: Cereal Rye Cover Crop Management for Corn and Soybean, AY-356-W
author_or_institution: Johnson, K., Camberato, J., and Legleiter, T.
limitations: Late spring termination after heading significantly increases stover C:N ratio and N tie-up.

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Consumptive Water Use (ETc) & Peak Water Extraction
recorded_value_or_summary: ETc 150-280 mm as cover crop terminated at boot; 380-550 mm full grain; peak daily ETc 4.0-6.5 mm/day during jointing-heading.
source_organization: FAO / Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education (SARE)
source_title: Crop Evapotranspiration (FAO 56) & Managing Cover Crops Profitably (3rd ed.)
author_or_institution: Allen, R.G. et al. (FAO) / Clark, A. (SARE)
limitations: In semiarid western Corn Belt, late spring termination can deplete profile moisture for succeeding corn.

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Root Architecture: Effective Water Extraction vs Maximum Anatomical Depth
recorded_value_or_summary: Effective water extraction depth 90-120 cm; maximum anatomical root depth 150-210 cm in friable soils.
source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & Root Development of Field Crops (Weaver 1926)
limitations: Dense claypans (argillic horizons) restrict rooting to upper 60-90 cm.

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Nutrient Uptake & Grain Nutrient Removal Standards
recorded_value_or_summary: Grain removal: 1.00 lb N/bu (17.9 kg N/t), 0.35 lb P2O5/bu (6.3 kg P2O5/t), 0.30 lb K2O/bu (5.4 kg K2O/t); Total uptake: 1.60 lb N/bu, 0.55 lb P2O5/bu, 1.45 lb K2O/bu.
source_organization: Tri-State / Kansas State University Agricultural Experiment Station
source_title: Tri-State Fertilizer Recommendations (Bul. 974) & KSU Rye Nutrient Data
author_or_institution: Culman, S. et al. (Tri-State) / Mengel, D.
limitations: Removal applies to grain harvest only; terminated cover crop exports 0.0 kg nutrients.

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Salinity Tolerance Threshold & Yield Decline Slope
recorded_value_or_summary: Salinity threshold EC_e = 2.5-3.5 dS/m; yield decline slope 10.0% per dS/m; moderately tolerant.
source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance: Current Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977)
citation_location: J. Irrig. Drainage Div. ASCE 103:115-134, Table 2
limitations: Emergence stage is more sensitive to salinity than vegetative growth.

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Cold Hardiness & Extreme Minimum Survival Temperature
recorded_value_or_summary: Survives down to -30 to -35°C under snow cover; -25°C bare soil; germination down to 1-2°C; lowest base temp (0.0-2.0°C) of all cereals.
source_organization: Crop Science Society of America / Univ. of Saskatchewan
source_title: Cold Acclimation and Low Temperature Tolerance of Cereal Crops
limitations: Unacclimated rapid freeze shocks cause crown injury at higher temperatures (-12°C).

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Heat Stress Sensitivity During Heading and Grain Filling
recorded_value_or_summary: Heat stress threshold 30.0-32.0°C; floret abortion and accelerated senescence occur above 32°C.
source_title: Heat Unit Concepts and Stress in Small Grains
limitations: Cover crops terminated at boot avoid reproductive summer heat stress entirely.

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Aboveground Biomass Production & Erosion Protection
recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass 3,000-6,500 kg/ha dry matter at boot to early heading; up to 8,000-10,000 kg/ha at maturity; reduces erosion by 60-90%.
source_title: Cereal Rye Cover Crop and Water Quality in the Midwest
author_or_institution: Kaspar, T.C., Jaynes, D.B., Parkin, T.B., and Moorman, T.B.
limitations: Biomass varies dramatically with spring termination timing (1.5 Mg/ha at Feekes 4 vs 6.5 Mg/ha at Feekes 10.5).

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Nitrate Scavenging Capacity & Groundwater Protection
recorded_value_or_summary: Scavenges 40-120 kg N/ha of residual fall soil nitrate; reduces subsurface drainage nitrate-N loss by 30-55%.
source_title: Reducing Nitrate Leaching in the Corn Belt with Cereal Rye
limitations: Captured nitrogen is recycled organically; not all is immediately plant-available to the next crop.

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye C:N Ratio Progression, Stover Decomposition & Spring N Immobilization
recorded_value_or_summary: C:N ratio 20:1-30:1 at jointing, 40:1-50:1 at boot, 65:1-85:1 at maturity; late termination immobilizes 20-40 lb N/ac.
source_organization: Soil Science Society of America / USDA-ARS
source_title: Time of Desiccation Effects on Plant Composition and Nitrogen Release from Rye
limitations: Successor corn requires starter N (20-40 lb N/ac) to offset early-season microbial tie-up.

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye Allelopathy: Benzoxazinoid Biosynthesis & Weed Suppression
recorded_value_or_summary: Synthesizes DIBOA and BOA in root exudates and shoots; suppresses small-seeded broadleaf weeds (pigweeds, waterhemp, lambsquarters).
source_organization: Journal of Chemical Ecology / Michigan State University
source_title: Role of Benzoxazinones in Allelopathy of Cereal Rye
limitations: Allelopathy does not control established perennial weeds or large-seeded cocklebur/morningglory.

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye to Corn Green Bridge & Seedling Pathogen Dynamics
recorded_value_or_summary: Live rye roots harbor Pythium and Fusarium; requires 10-14 day termination window before corn planting to avoid seedling blight.
source_organization: The American Phytopathological Society / Iowa State Univ.
source_title: Green Bridge Dynamics and Corn Seedling Disease after Cereal Rye Termination
author_or_institution: Acharya, J., Bakker, M.G., Moorman, T.B., and Robertson, A.E.
limitations: Planting green is viable for soybean, but poses severe seedling disease risk for corn unless fungicide-treated and warm.

attribute_or_claim: Cereal Rye-to-Soybean Rotational Synergy & Weed Suppression Performance
recorded_value_or_summary: Highly compatible rotation; rye mulch suppresses Palmer amaranth and waterhemp; soybean fixes own N bypassing C:N immobilization.
source_organization: American Society of Agronomy / Univ. of Missouri / MCCC
source_title: Cereal Rye Preceding Soybean: Agronomic and Economic Performance
limitations: In drought years, excessive late rye growth can deplete seed zone moisture if not monitored.

attribute_or_claim: Botanical Taxonomy, Ploidy & Non-Vernalizing Habit of Common Oats
recorded_value_or_summary: Avena sativa L., Poaceae, allohexaploid (2n=6x=42), cool-season annual; vernalization not required for spring cultivars; 80-110 d grain.
source_title: The PLANTS Database: Avena sativa L.
limitations: Spring types dominate Midwest/Plains; winter types adapted only to USDA hardiness zones 7-9.

attribute_or_claim: Spring Oat Growth Stages & Growing Degree Day Accumulation
recorded_value_or_summary: GDD base 4.4°C (40°F); cumulative GDD to grain maturity 1300-1700 GDD; 80-110 days active growth duration.
source_organization: University of Minnesota Extension / NDSU Extension
source_title: Growing Oats in the Upper Midwest & Small Grain Phenology
geographic_scope: Northern Corn Belt & Northern Great Plains
limitations: Seeding past early May in the Midwest leads to severe yield and test weight reductions from summer heat.

attribute_or_claim: Oat Consumptive Water Use (ETc) & Peak Daily Flux Rates
recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 350-500 mm for grain, 150-250 mm for fall cover; peak daily water use 4.0-6.0 mm/day at heading.
source_title: Yield Response to Water (FAO Irrigation Paper 33 & 56)
author_or_institution: Doorenbos, J. and Kassam, A.H. / Allen, R.G. et al.
limitations: Higher transpiration ratio than barley or wheat; more susceptible to late-season terminal drought.

attribute_or_claim: Oat Root Architecture: Effective Extraction Depth vs Maximum Penetration
recorded_value_or_summary: Effective water extraction depth 70-100 cm; maximum anatomical root depth 120-150 cm; >75% of root mass in top 45 cm.
source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & Root Development of Field Crops (Weaver 1926)
limitations: Root depth is shallower than winter rye or winter wheat.

attribute_or_claim: Oat Grain Removal Standards & Total Crop Nutrient Uptake
recorded_value_or_summary: Grain removal: 0.65 lb N/bu (18.6 kg N/t), 0.25 lb P2O5/bu (7.2 kg P2O5/t), 0.20 lb K2O/bu (5.7 kg K2O/t); Total uptake: 1.10 lb N/bu.
source_title: Tri-State Fertilizer Recommendations, Bulletin 974
limitations: Straw baling and removal exports an additional 25-35 lb K2O/acre.

attribute_or_claim: Oat Salinity Tolerance Threshold & Yield Decline Slope
recorded_value_or_summary: Salinity threshold EC_e = 3.0-4.0 dS/m; yield decline slope 10.0% per dS/m; moderately tolerant.
source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance: Current Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977)
citation_location: J. Irrig. Drainage Div. ASCE 103:115-134, Table 2
limitations: More salt-tolerant than corn or soybean, but significantly less tolerant than barley.

attribute_or_claim: Spring Oat Winter-Kill Threshold & Fall Cover Crop Termination Mechanism
recorded_value_or_summary: Winter-kills reliably at -7.0 to -9.0°C (15-20°F) consecutive freeze; zero spring chemical termination required.
source_title: Cover Crops for Conservation Tillage Systems & Managing Cover Crops Profitably
limitations: Winter-kill does not occur reliably in USDA zones 8-10, where oats survive winter as annual forage.

attribute_or_claim: Oat Thermal Sensitivity During Boot to Anthesis: Heat Breakpoint
recorded_value_or_summary: Heat stress threshold 28.0-30.0°C; temperatures >28°C during heading induce floret blasting and reduce test weight (<32 lb/bu).
source_organization: Field Crops Research / MTT Agrifood Research
source_title: Heat and Drought Sensitivity of Oats under Temperate Climates
author_or_institution: Peltonen-Sainio, P., Rajala, A., and Jauhiainen, L.
limitations: Fall cover crops avoid summer heat stress completely.

attribute_or_claim: Fall Oat Cover Crop Biomass Accumulation & Soil Erosion Reduction
recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass 2,500-5,000 kg/ha dry matter in fall before winterkill; provides rapid 80-95% canopy cover within 40-50 days.
source_title: Managing Cover Crops Profitably & Fall Cover Crop Trials
limitations: Seeding after September 15 in the Upper Midwest results in <1.0 ton/acre biomass due to thermal constraints.

attribute_or_claim: Oats as a Companion Nurse Crop for Perennial Legume Establishment
recorded_value_or_summary: Standard companion crop for alfalfa and red clover; suppresses weeds, protects soil, harvested at boot as oatlage or July as grain.
source_title: Forage and Small Grain Establishment Guides, Extension Bulletin A2809
author_or_institution: Undersander, D., Cosgrove, D., and Cullen, E.
limitations: Oats must be cut early (boot stage) in drought years to prevent excessive soil moisture competition with young alfalfa seedlings.

attribute_or_claim: Winter-Killed Oat Residue C:N Dynamics & Rapid Spring Decomposition
recorded_value_or_summary: Residue C:N ratio 20:1-35:1 at freeze; decomposes rapidly in early spring; causes minimal spring N immobilization (<10 lb N/ac).
source_organization: Canadian Journal of Soil Science / Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada
source_title: Residue Decomposition and Nutrient Release of Annual Cereals
limitations: Mature oat straw harvested for grain has higher C:N (45:1 to 60:1).

attribute_or_claim: Oat Sensitivity to Sulfonylurea and Triazine Herbicide Carryover
recorded_value_or_summary: Highly sensitive to atrazine, fomesafen, and sulfonylurea (e.g. chlorimuron) soil residues; plant-back interval 10-18 months.
source_title: Illinois Weed Control Guide & Herbicide Carryover Tables
citation_location: Illinois Agricultural Pest Management Handbook, Chapter 2
limitations: Check specific product master labels for regional rotational restrictions.

attribute_or_claim: Winter-Killed Oats Preceding Corn: Clean Seedbed & Zero Green Bridge
recorded_value_or_summary: Highly compatible predecessor to corn; leaves a mellow, friable seedbed with zero green bridge, no insect vectoring, and no soil drying.
source_organization: Iowa State University Extension / Purdue Extension
source_title: Cover Crops for Modern Cropping Systems, PM 1714
limitations: Provides less spring weed suppression than an overwintering rye cover crop.

attribute_or_claim: U.S. Commercial Oat Planting and Harvesting Date Windows Across Regions
recorded_value_or_summary: Midwest/Plains planting March 25 - April 30, harvest July 15 - August 20; Southern forage planting Sept 15 - Oct 31.
source_title: Field Crops: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates, Agricultural Handbook 628
limitations: Severe spring wetness can delay planting into May, reducing grain yields.

attribute_or_claim: Botanical Taxonomy, Ploidy & Perennial Longevity of Alfalfa
recorded_value_or_summary: Medicago sativa L., Fabaceae, autotetraploid (2n=4x=32), perennial forage legume; stand duration 3-5 yr (up to 7+ yr in West).
source_title: The PLANTS Database: Medicago sativa L.
limitations: Stands thin naturally due to crown diseases and traffic after 4-6 years.

attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Multi-Cutting Phenology, Cutting Intervals & Fall Dormancy Classes
recorded_value_or_summary: GDD base 5.0°C; 3-5 cuttings/yr in Midwest, 6-8 in Southwest; 28-35 day cutting interval at early bud to 1/10 bloom; FD 1-11.
source_organization: University of Wisconsin / Minnesota / Iowa State Extension
source_title: Alfalfa Management Guide (NCR 547)
limitations: Frequent cutting before bud stage severely depletes crown carbohydrates, leading to stand death.

attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Consumptive Water Use (ETc) & High Irrigation Demand
recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 600-1200 mm/yr; peak daily flux 6.0-9.0 mm/day; net irrigation requirement 400-900 mm in arid/semi-arid regions.
source_organization: FAO / University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
source_title: Crop Evapotranspiration (FAO 56) & Alfalfa Water Management (ANR Pub 8262)
author_or_institution: Allen, R.G. et al. (FAO) / Hanson, B., Putnam, D., and Snyder, R.
citation_location: UC ANR Publication 8262, pp. 1-12; FAO 56 Table 12
limitations: One of the highest seasonal water-consuming field crops in North America.

attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Taproot Depth: Effective Extraction vs Maximum Bio-Drilling Depth
recorded_value_or_summary: Effective water extraction depth 120-180 cm; maximum anatomical root depth 250-350 cm (documented up to 500-600 cm in deep alluvium).
source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & Root Development of Field Crops (Weaver 1926)
citation_location: NEH Part 652 Chapter 3; Weaver (1926) Chapter 18, pp. 215-240
limitations: Acid subsoils (pH <5.5) or high water tables severely restrict taproot elongation.

attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Forage Nutrient Removal & Heavy Soil Potassium Depletion
recorded_value_or_summary: Forage removal: 50-65 lb N/ton (2.5-3.2% N), 12-15 lb P2O5/ton, 45-60 lb K2O/ton dry hay; massive potassium mining.
source_title: Tri-State Fertilizer Recommendations, Bulletin 974
limitations: Failure to apply potassium causes rapid stand thinning and winterkill.

attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Salinity Tolerance Threshold & Yield Decline Rate
recorded_value_or_summary: Salinity threshold EC_e = 2.0 dS/m; yield decline slope 7.3% per dS/m; moderately sensitive.
source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance: Current Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977)
citation_location: J. Irrig. Drainage Div. ASCE 103:115-134, Table 2
limitations: Seedling emergence stage is twice as sensitive to salinity as established plants.

attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Crown Freezing Tolerance & Critical Winter Survival Limits
recorded_value_or_summary: Air survival to -20 to -25°C under snow; lethal soil crown temperature -10 to -15°C (14 to 5°F) at 2-4 cm depth.
source_organization: Canadian Journal of Plant Science / Univ. of Wisconsin
source_title: Freezing Resistance and Carbohydrate Composition in Alfalfa
author_or_institution: McKenzie, J.S. et al. / Undersander, D.
limitations: Cutting during the critical fall rest period (6 weeks prior to killing frost) increases winterkill risk.

attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa High Temperature Heat Stress & Summer Slump Phenomenon
recorded_value_or_summary: Heat stress threshold 32.0-35.0°C; night temps >20°C accelerate dark respiration, reducing forage yield and digestibility.
source_organization: Environmental and Experimental Botany / Univ. of Minnesota
source_title: Alfalfa Physiology and High Temperature Response
author_or_institution: Erice, G. et al. / Sheaffer, C.C.
limitations: Non-dormant southwestern cultivars tolerate higher temperatures than northern dormant types.

attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Symbiotic Nitrogen Fixation by Sinorhizobium meliloti
recorded_value_or_summary: Sinorhizobium meliloti symbiosis; %Ndfa 70-90%; fixes 150-350 kg N/ha/yr (up to 400+ kg N/ha/yr in irrigated west).
source_title: Symbiotic Nitrogen Fixation in Alfalfa (Heichel et al. 1984 & Vance 2002)
author_or_institution: Vance, C.P. / Heichel, G.H. et al.
limitations: Acid soils (pH <6.2) severely reduce nodule formation and nitrogenase enzyme activity.

attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Successor Fertilizer-N Credit to Corn: Year 1 and Year 2 Dynamics
recorded_value_or_summary: First-year N credit 100-150 lb N/ac (110-170 kg N/ha) to corn; second-year carryover credit 30-50 lb N/ac (35-55 kg N/ha).
source_organization: Journal of Production Agriculture / Univ. of Wisconsin / Iowa State Univ.
source_title: Fertilizer N Equivalence of Alfalfa for Succeeding Corn & Extension Guidelines
author_or_institution: Fox, R.H. and Piekielek, W.P. / Undersander, D. / Sawyer, J.
citation_location: J. Prod. Agric. 1:313-317; UW A2809; ISU PM 1714
limitations: Poor stands (<2 plants/ft2) provide lower credits (60-80 lb N/ac); sandy soils experience rapid leaching.

attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Autotoxicity: Medicarpin Exudation & Rotational Break Requirement
recorded_value_or_summary: Medicarpin and phenolic root exudates inhibit seedling germination; requires 12-24 month rotational break before reseeding.
source_title: Zone of Autotoxic Influence Around Established Alfalfa Plants
limitations: Interseeding into stands <1 year old is viable; stands >2 years old exhibit severe autotoxicity.

attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa Strict Soil pH Sensitivity & Aluminum Toxicity Threshold
recorded_value_or_summary: Optimal pH 6.5-7.5; tolerated 6.0-8.0; below pH 6.2 Sinorhizobium nodulation fails and aluminum impairs taproot growth.
source_organization: Soil Fertility and Fertilizers / Univ. of Wisconsin Extension
source_title: Soil Fertility and Fertilizers (8th ed.) & Alfalfa Management Guide
author_or_institution: Havlin, J.L. et al. / Undersander, D. et al.
citation_location: NCR 547 pp. 8-11; Havlin et al. Chapter 6
limitations: Topsoil liming does not immediately neutralize acidic subsoils, which continue to impede deep taprooting.

attribute_or_claim: Alfalfa-to-Corn Rotational Synergies: Yield Premium & Rootworm Break
recorded_value_or_summary: Highly compatible rotation; 10-15% corn yield premium over continuous corn; complete biological break for corn rootworm.
source_organization: Purdue University Extension / Univ. of Wisconsin
source_title: Corn Rotational Response Following Alfalfa & NCR 547
author_or_institution: Camberato, J. and Nielsen, R.L. / Undersander, D.
limitations: Excessive early spring alfalfa growth must be terminated before it depletes topsoil moisture for corn emergence.

attribute_or_claim: U.S. Alfalfa Production Systems Across Midwest Dairy, Western Irrigated & Plains
recorded_value_or_summary: Midwest/Northeast 3-5 cuttings rainfed; Western irrigated (CA, ID) 6-8+ cuttings; Northern Plains dryland 2-3 cuttings.
source_title: Field Crops: Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates, Agricultural Handbook 628
limitations: Western systems depend almost entirely on irrigation water rights.

attribute_or_claim: Botanical Taxonomy, Climbing Habit & Cover Crop Role of Hairy Vetch
recorded_value_or_summary: Vicia villosa Roth, Fabaceae, diploid (2n=14), winter annual climbing legume; 210-270 d duration; premier winter cover crop.
source_title: The PLANTS Database: Vicia villosa Roth
limitations: Produces hard seed if allowed to mature, creating volunteer weed issues in small grains.

attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Phenology, Spring Biomass Surge & Optimal Termination Timing
recorded_value_or_summary: GDD base 4.0°C; 1100-1600 GDD to 50% bloom; optimal roller-crimper termination at 50-100% bloom (May); 210-270 d.
source_title: Managing Cover Crops Profitably (3rd ed.)
limitations: Premature termination (<50% bloom) leads to incomplete kill with roller-crimpers.

attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Biomass Production, Spring Soil Moisture Dynamics & Nitrogen Accumulation
recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass accumulation 3.0-5.5 Mg/ha; spring moisture extraction reaches 4.5-6.5 mm/day at flowering; rapid biomass accumulation provides substantial soil cover.
source_title: Potential Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reduction through No-Till Cover-Crop Systems
author_or_institution: Teasdale, J.R., Coffman, C.B., and Mangum, R.W.
limitations: Spring moisture depletion occurs primarily when termination is delayed into full bloom under low-rainfall conditions. FAO 56 crop coefficients provide generalized reference evapotranspiration multipliers.

attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Root Architecture: Effective Extraction vs Maximum Depth
recorded_value_or_summary: Branched taproot; effective water extraction depth 75-100 cm; maximum anatomical depth 120-150 cm; dense nodules in top 30 cm.
source_title: National Engineering Handbook Part 652 & Root Development of Field Crops (Weaver 1926)
limitations: Waterlogged or compacted subsoils severely restrict lateral branching and nodule aeration.

attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Aboveground Biomass Accumulation & Tissue Nitrogen Content
recorded_value_or_summary: Biomass 3,000-6,000 kg/ha dry matter by 50% bloom; tissue nitrogen concentration 3.0-4.2% N (high succulent protein).
source_title: Growth and Nitrogen Accumulation of Hairy Vetch Cover Crops
limitations: Early April termination yields <2.0 Mg/ha biomass and <60 kg N/ha.

attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Salinity Tolerance Threshold & Yield Decline Rate
recorded_value_or_summary: Salinity threshold EC_e = 1.5-2.5 dS/m; yield decline slope 12.0% per dS/m; moderately sensitive.
source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance: Current Assessment (Maas & Hoffman 1977)
citation_location: J. Irrig. Drainage Div. ASCE 103:115-134, Table 2
limitations: Not suitable for saline-sodic soils in the semiarid West.

attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Winter Hardiness & Extreme Cold Survival Temperature
recorded_value_or_summary: Survives down to -15.0 to -20.0°C (0 to -4°F) with snow; base temperature 4.0°C; most winter-hardy annual legume in US.
source_organization: Norwegian Journal of Agricultural Sciences / USDA-ARS
source_title: Winter Survival of Hairy Vetch and Other Annual Legumes
author_or_institution: Brandsaeter, L.O. et al. / Teasdale, J.R.
limitations: Late-seeded small seedlings (<3 leaves) winterkill during severe bare-ground freezes.

attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Heat Stress Threshold & Late Spring Senescence
recorded_value_or_summary: Heat stress threshold 30.0-32.0°C; high temperatures in late spring accelerate senescence and terminate vegetative growth.
source_title: Managing Cover Crops Profitably & Organic No-Till Trials
limitations: Requires termination before seed maturation to prevent weed problems.

attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Symbiotic Nitrogen Fixation by Rhizobium leguminosarum bv. viciae
recorded_value_or_summary: Rhizobium leguminosarum bv. viciae; %Ndfa 70-85%; fixes 90-200 kg N/ha (80-180 lb N/ac); net soil N balance +90 to +200 kg N/ha.
source_title: Nitrogen Fixation by Winter Cover Legumes
author_or_institution: Power, J.F., Doran, J.W., and Koerner, P.T.
limitations: High residual mineral soil N (>80 kg N/ha) depresses nodulation and fixation percentage.

attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Successor Fertilizer-N Credit to Corn and Sorghum
recorded_value_or_summary: Fertilizer replacement credit 60-120 lb N/ac (65-135 kg N/ha); directly reduces synthetic N fertilizer requirements for corn/sorghum.
source_title: Cover Crop Nitrogen Contributions to Corn & Agronomy Facts 53
author_or_institution: Teasdale, J.R. et al. / Curran, W.
citation_location: Agron. J. 96(6):1572-1581; Penn State Agronomy Facts 53
limitations: Credit drops to 30-50 lb N/ac if terminated early (mid-April) due to reduced biomass accumulation.

attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch C:N Ratio & Explosive Spring Mineralization Kinetics
recorded_value_or_summary: C:N ratio 10:1-15:1; succulent tissue releases 50-75% of total nitrogen within 3-4 weeks post-termination; zero immobilization.
source_organization: Soil Science Society of America Journal / North Carolina State Univ.
source_title: Nitrogen Release from Crimson Clover and Hairy Vetch
limitations: Rapid N release can lead to leaching losses if heavy rainfall occurs before corn root establishment.

attribute_or_claim: Roller-Crimper Termination Efficacy & Hard Seed Weed Risk in Small Grains
recorded_value_or_summary: Mechanical roller-crimper requires 50-100% bloom for >90% kill; mature hard seed causes severe weed infestation in wheat/barley.
source_title: Hairy Vetch Management for No-Till Organic Corn Production
limitations: Do not rotate hairy vetch before winter wheat or barley if any seed pods have matured.

attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch Host Status for Root-Knot and Soybean Cyst Nematodes
recorded_value_or_summary: Susceptible reproductive host to Meloidogyne incognita and Heterodera glycines; caution before cotton, soybean, or tobacco.
source_title: Evaluation of Winter Cover Crops as Hosts for Meloidogyne incognita
author_or_institution: Timper, P., Davis, R.F., and Tillman, P.G.
limitations: Do not plant hairy vetch in fields with active root-knot nematode infestations preceding susceptible cash crops.

attribute_or_claim: Hairy Vetch to Corn and Sorghum Rotational Synergies & Weed Mulch
recorded_value_or_summary: Highly compatible rotation; provides 60-120 lb N/ac, thick in-situ residue mulch suppresses early weeds, boosts corn yield by 10-20%.
source_title: Bio-Economic Evaluation of No-Till Corn Following Hairy Vetch
limitations: Vetch vines can wrap around planter wheels if not properly rolled or chemically desiccated.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Botanical Identity, Morphology & Functional Classification
recorded_value_or_summary: Trifolium incarnatum L. (TRIN3); Fabaceae; erect annual bunchgrass-like legume (0.3-0.8 m); dark green pilose trifoliolate leaves; elongated scarlet conical flower heads (2.5-6.0 cm); non-stoloniferous.
source_title: The PLANTS Database — Trifolium incarnatum L.
limitations: Taxonomic baseline; morphological height and tiller development vary with seeding density and spring temperature.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Phenology, Thermal Base & Growing Degree Day Accumulation
recorded_value_or_summary: Active growth 180-240 days (winter annual) or 60-90 days (spring-seeded north); base temperature 4.0-5.0°C; 1000-1500 GDD accumulated to full bloom.
source_title: Managing Cover Crops Profitably (3rd ed.)
limitations: GDD accumulation varies by planting date and cultivar dormancy characteristics.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Cold Hardiness, Winter Survival Limits & Frost-Heaving Dynamics
recorded_value_or_summary: Absolute minimum survival -12°C to -15°C (10°F to 5°F) with snow cover; winter-kills below -15°C to -18°C on bare soil; vulnerable to freeze-thaw frost-heaving.
source_organization: Purdue University Extension / Midwest Cover Crops Council
source_title: Crimson Clover Cover Crop for Midwestern Systems
author_or_institution: Midwest Cover Crops Council / Purdue Extension
limitations: Late-planted clover with <4 leaves suffers 100% winter-kill below -10°C.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Consumptive Water Use (ETc) & Soil Moisture Depletion
recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 250-400 mm; peak daily water use 3.5-5.5 mm/day during late vegetative and bloom stages in April-May; moderate-to-low drought tolerance.
source_title: Crop Evapotranspiration: Guidelines for Computing Crop Water Requirements
author_or_institution: Allen, R.G., Pereira, L.S., Raes, D., and Smith, M.
citation_location: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56, Table 12
limitations: Delayed spring termination in dry years desiccates seedbed for subsequent corn or cotton.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Soil pH Boundaries, Acidity Sensitivity & Salinity Threshold
recorded_value_or_summary: Optimal soil pH 6.0-7.0 (tolerates 5.5-7.5); highly sensitive to aluminum toxicity at pH <5.2; sensitive to salinity (ECe threshold 1.5-2.0 dS/m).
source_organization: U.S. Salinity Laboratory / John Wiley & Sons
source_title: Crop Salt Tolerance — Current Assessment & Soil Fertility Management
author_or_institution: Maas, E.V. and Hoffman, G.J. / Havlin, J.L. et al.
citation_location: ASCE J. Irrig. Drain. Div. 103(2):115-134; Soil Fertility and Fertilizers 8th ed.
limitations: Liming strongly improves nodulation on acid Southeastern ultisols.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Root System Architecture & Effective Water Extraction Depth
recorded_value_or_summary: Branched fibrous taproot; effective water extraction depth 40-70 cm; maximum anatomical root depth 80-120 cm; low-to-moderate compaction alleviation.
source_title: Root Development of Field Crops & National Engineering Handbook Part 652
citation_location: Root Development of Field Crops, Chapter 19; NEH Part 652, Table 3-4
limitations: Root depth is severely restricted by dense subsoil fragipans or high water tables.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Symbiotic Biological Nitrogen Fixation & Rhizobium Specificity
recorded_value_or_summary: Symbiont: Rhizobium leguminosarum bv. trifolii (Type R); fixes 70-150 kg N/ha (60-135 lb N/ac); 60-80% Ndfa under optimal nodulation.
source_organization: North Carolina State University Extension / SARE
source_title: Winter Annual Legumes for Conservation Tillage
author_or_institution: Ranells, N.N., Wagger, M.G., and Hoyt, G.D.
limitations: High soil nitrate levels (>25 ppm) suppress nodulation and reduce %Ndfa.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Biomass Yield, Tissue N Concentration & C:N Decomposition Kinetics
recorded_value_or_summary: Dry matter biomass 2,500-5,500 kg/ha; tissue N concentration 2.5-3.8%; C:N ratio 12:1 to 18:1; rapid residue mineralization releasing 50% N in 3-5 weeks.
source_title: Nitrogen Release from Crimson Clover in Relation to Plant Maturity and Decomposition
limitations: Delaying termination to late seed maturity increases C:N ratio to >22:1, slowing decomposition.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Rotational Nitrogen Replacement Credit to Succeeding Cash Crops
recorded_value_or_summary: Fertilizer-N replacement credit 40-80 lb N/ac (45-90 kg N/ha) to corn, sorghum, or cotton; zero microbial N immobilization; rapid early mineralization.
source_organization: American Society of Agronomy / Auburn University
source_title: Review of Fertilizer Nitrogen Credits for Crimson Clover in Conservation Tillage
author_or_institution: Torbert, H.A., Reeves, D.W., and Mulvaney, R.L.
citation_location: J. Prod. Agric. 9(1):95-100; Auburn Ext. Circular ANR-1311
limitations: Credit declines to 20-30 lb N/ac if clover stand is sparse (<50% ground cover) or terminated prematurely.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Mechanical Termination via Roller-Crimper & Regrowth Constraints
recorded_value_or_summary: Roller-crimper termination requires >=75-100% full bloom for complete kill; rolling at vegetative or early bud stage results in 40-60% regrowth.
source_title: Hairy Vetch and Crimson Clover Management for No-Till Organic Corn
author_or_institution: Mischler, R.A., Duiker, S.W., Curran, W.S., and Wilson, D.
limitations: In conventional systems, glyphosate or 2,4-D/dicamba burndown allows earlier vegetative termination.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Soil Coverage, Erosion Control & Aggregate Stabilization
recorded_value_or_summary: Rapid canopy closure provides 85-98% ground cover by mid-spring; reduces rainfall runoff by 40-65% and sediment erosion by 60-80% compared to winter fallow.
source_title: Restoration of Degraded Soils with Cover Crops in the Southeastern USA
author_or_institution: Langdale, G.W., Blevins, R.L., Karlen, D.L., et al.
limitations: Slow early-autumn growth on late-planted fields leaves soil vulnerable to early-winter sheet erosion.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Host Status for Nematodes, Crown Rot Pathogens & Corn Rootworm Break
recorded_value_or_summary: Non-host biological break for Corn Rootworm; host to Meloidogyne incognita (Southern Root-Knot Nematode) and Sclerotinia trifoliorum (clover rot); weak host to SCN.
source_organization: Organization of Nematologists of Tropical America (ONTA)
source_title: Evaluation of Cover Crops as Hosts for Root-Knot Nematodes (Meloidogyne spp.)
author_or_institution: Timper, P., Davis, R.F., and Tillotson, D.K.
limitations: In cold-winter northern zones, low soil temperatures suppress winter nematode reproduction.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Rotational Synergies with Corn, Sorghum & Cotton
recorded_value_or_summary: Supplies 40-80 lb N/ac and 8-14% yield premium to subsequent corn and cotton in conservation tillage; breaks grass disease cycles.
source_title: Cover Crops and Rotations for Conservation Tillage Systems
limitations: Spring moisture depletion requires timely termination in sub-humid production regions.

attribute_or_claim: Crimson Clover Regional Adaptation, Hardiness Zones & Reseeding Management
recorded_value_or_summary: Premier winter annual cover crop across USDA Zones 6b-9; adapted to Coastal Plain, Piedmont, Mid-South, and Ohio Valley; summer annual in Zone 4-5.
source_title: Crimson Clover in Conservation Tillage Systems
author_or_institution: Hancock, D.W., Durham, R.G., and Cabrera, M.L.
limitations: Reseeding cultivars create volunteer weed risks in subsequent winter small grain crops.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Botanical Identity, Brassicaceae Classification & Non-Fixing Habit
recorded_value_or_summary: Raphanus sativus L. (RASA2); Brassicaceae; cool-season annual; basal rosette of lyrate leaves with swollen cylindrical taproot (15-35 cm); non-legume (0.0 kg N/ha BNF).
source_title: The PLANTS Database — Raphanus sativus L.
limitations: Cultivars selected for cover cropping (daikon/oilseed) differ from culinary radishes in taproot elongation and glucosinolate profile.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Phenology, Thermal Base & Rapid Autumn Growth Cycle
recorded_value_or_summary: Active growth duration 50-75 days (late summer to winter-kill); base temperature 3.0-4.0°C; 600-1000 GDD accumulated; photoperiod bolting sensitivity.
source_organization: American Society of Agronomy / Michigan State University
source_title: Evaluating Cover Crops for Benefits, Costs and Performance within Diverse Cropping Systems
author_or_institution: Snapp, S.S., Date, K., and Kirk, W.
limitations: Early summer seedings bolt prematurely in response to long days, producing woody stalks and reduced fleshy taproots.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Winter-Kill Temperature Thresholds & Complete Biomass Collapse
recorded_value_or_summary: Winter-kills reliably at sustained temperatures below -6°C to -9°C (21°F to 15°F) for >=4-6 hours; cellular ice crystallization causes complete root collapse.
source_title: Thinking about Cover Crops? Think Radish
citation_location: UMD Extension Fact Sheet FS-824, pp. 1-6
limitations: In USDA Zones 8-9 (Deep South/California), mild winters prevent reliable winter-kill, requiring chemical burndown.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Subsoil Compaction Alleviation & Bio-Drilling Macropore Formation
recorded_value_or_summary: Thick fleshy taproot penetrates compacted subsoil layers (>2.0 MPa penetration resistance); winter decay creates open vertical macropores (2-5 cm wide, 1-2 m deep).
source_title: Penetration of Compact Subsoils by Diverse Cover Crop Roots
limitations: Compaction alleviation fails if soil is severely smeared, waterlogged, or if planting is delayed (<40 days of growth before freeze).

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Consumptive Water Use (ETc) & Infiltration Enhancement
recorded_value_or_summary: Seasonal ETc 150-300 mm over 60-day autumn window; peak daily water use 3.0-4.5 mm/day; winter-decay biopores increase water infiltration rates 2-3 fold.
source_title: Root Growth and Yield of Maize as Affected by Previous Cover Crops and Soil Compaction
limitations: Infiltration increases (2- to 3-fold) were measured in Maryland silt loam soils via constant-head permeameters in open winter-decay biopores (Chen & Weil 2011); benefit depends on presence of dense plow pan and uncollapsed biopores; rapid autumn water extraction can dry topsoil during droughty autumns.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Soil pH Preferences, Salinity Tolerance & Waterlogging Sensitivity
recorded_value_or_summary: Optimal soil pH 6.0-7.5 (tolerates 5.5-8.0); moderately tolerant to salinity (ECe threshold 3.0-4.0 dS/m); poor waterlogging tolerance (rots in standing water).
source_title: Tolerance of Vegetable and Brassica Crops to Salinity
limitations: Waterlogged clay soils result in stunted, unbranched, rotting taproots.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Fleshy Taproot Dimensions & Deep Anatomical Penetration
recorded_value_or_summary: Fleshy storage root 15-35 cm length, 2.5-7.0 cm diameter; fine vertical taproot penetrates 150-240 cm (5-8 ft); effective extraction depth 60-120 cm.
source_title: Root Development of Field Crops & Field Soil Studies
author_or_institution: Weaver, J.E. / Chen, G. and Weil, R.R.
citation_location: Root Development of Field Crops, Chapter 22; Soil & Tillage Res. 108:31-40
limitations: Extreme compaction (>3.5 MPa) restricts root elongation, forcing horizontal swelling.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Residual Nitrate Scavenging Capacity & Profile Recovery
recorded_value_or_summary: Exceptional autumn nitrate scavenger, capturing 100-220 kg N/ha (100-200 lb N/ac) from soil profile; reduces nitrate leaching to groundwater by 60-90%.
source_organization: American Society of Agronomy / Soil Science Society of America
source_title: Brassica Cover Crops for Nitrogen Scavenging in the Mid-Atlantic Coastal Plain
limitations: Total N scavenged depends strictly on available soil residual mineral N.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Biomass Yield, C:N Quality & Rapid Spring Decomposition
recorded_value_or_summary: Total dry matter 4,500-9,000 kg/ha (top: 3,000-6,000; root: 1,500-3,500); low C:N ratio (10:1 to 15:1); succulent tissue decomposes rapidly upon freezing.
source_title: Nitrogen Release Dynamics from Brassica Cover Crops
author_or_institution: Jahanzad, E., Barker, A.V., Hashemi, M., et al.
limitations: Rapid breakdown emits strong sulfurous/mercaptan odors in late winter.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Spring Nitrogen Release Kinetics & Leaching Vulnerability
recorded_value_or_summary: Releases 70-80% of captured N in March-April; on coarse sandy soils, early mineralized nitrate can leach before May corn uptake unless captured by companion grass.
source_organization: Soil Science Society of America / University of California
source_title: Tillage and Cover Crop Effects on Nitrogen Mineralization and Leaching Dynamics
author_or_institution: Veenstra, J.J., Horwath, W.R., and Mitchell, J.P.
limitations: Pairing radish with cereal rye effectively prevents early-spring nitrate loss.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Glucosinolates & Biofumigation Suppression of Soil Pathogens
recorded_value_or_summary: High glucosinolate content (4-methylthio-3-butenyl glucosinolate); enzymatic hydrolysis produces isothiocyanates (ITCs) that suppress soil fungi and nematodes.
source_organization: CSIRO Plant Industry / Kluwer Academic Publishers
source_title: Biofumigation Potential of Brassicas: Glucosinolate Profiles and Biological Activity
limitations: Glucosinolate biofumigation is a secondary, variable biological suppression mechanism observed primarily in vitro and in closed microplots (Kirkegaard & Sarwar 1998); natural winter-kill tissue release is diffuse and does not substitute for commercial fungicides or nematicides.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Pest Vulnerabilities, Clubroot Risk & Nematode Break
recorded_value_or_summary: Susceptible to Clubroot (Plasmodiophora brassicae), flea beetles, and cabbage looper; non-host biological break for Soybean Cyst Nematode (SCN).
source_title: Potential of Brassicaceous Cover Crops for Nematode Management
author_or_institution: Melakeberhan, H., Mennan, S., Chen, S., et al.
limitations: Susceptible host to Clubroot and flea beetles; non-host break for SCN (Melakeberhan et al. 2010). Caution is warranted when rotating with commercial brassicas (canola, broccoli, cabbage) in fields with Clubroot history or acidic soils (pH <6.8); requires 3- to 4-year rotational breaks and pH management rather than representing an automatic statutory prohibition.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Rotational Synergies with Corn, Soybean & Small Grains
recorded_value_or_summary: Precedes corn and soybean with 5-10% yield bump on compacted soils; ideal after winter wheat/barley; requires high caution preceding commercial brassicas due to shared Clubroot risk; creates mellow seedbed.
source_title: Oilseed Radish: A Versatile Cover Crop for Michigan
limitations: Corn yield increase (5-10%) is conditional on compacted no-till soils where radish biopores relieve subsoil physical impedance (Chen & Weil 2011; MSU E-3165); response is negligible on loose uncompacted soils. Requires planting within 1-2 weeks of wheat/barley harvest (August) for maximum root mass.

attribute_or_claim: Oilseed Radish Rapid Canopy Closure, Weed Suppression & Odor Dynamics
recorded_value_or_summary: Achieves 100% canopy cover in 3-4 weeks; suppresses fall and early-spring winter annual weeds (marestail, chickweed); sulfurous decay odor during spring thaw.
source_organization: Weed Science Society of America / USDA-ARS
source_title: Forage Radish Cover Crop Suppresses Winter Annual Weeds in Fall and Early Spring
author_or_institution: Lawley, Y.E., Weil, R.R., and Teasdale, J.R.
limitations: Weed suppression declines rapidly by late April as radish residue decomposes completely.
